title: Cardiac surgery network: remote monitoring cost and effect, four-centre cohort, late audit reply refused
notes: Level 5 expert path: a multi-site design, a family change only on acceptance, dependency closure between protocol and stats, and a late audit reply refused after an investigator edit. The need asks for a cost-effectiveness analysis (routing explicit 'economic'). The problem reply sends constraints null: under G11 the typed constraints stay and the attempt is recorded as rejected-change (S5). Seven fixture records are appraised (five claims, one of high uncertainty). The design reply recommends 'cohort' because the missing input for the economic question is a fair effect estimate; the proposed recommendation does not change the family (D3 under S11), and acceptance of the supported decision sets family 'cohort' with basis 'explicit' while the unknown centre D cost gate keeps the action blocked. After Protocol, Stats and Ethics are complete, protocol call 2 revises the comparison period for a contaminated comparison centre; Stats and Ethics are flagged 'review required' (G8); stats call 2 clears Stats and the investigator marks Ethics complete by hand. At the Audit stage, the first reply is held while the investigator edits the audit notes and is then refused (G6): encoded as illuminate (request sent, reply held) then set-field then wait (reply delivered), because the format has no field for a held reply. A fresh audit call is applied and omits improvementNotes, so the investigator's note stays. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59, computed by the generator: DOI-keyed for records 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 (ev-0gdg3o5, ev-0p8nj5i, ev-0fos45w, ev-0f46h0m, ev-0xbcx1h) and titleYearKey-keyed for records 2 and 7 (ev-1wngjtj, ev-1w2yv8t). Requires S5 (rejected-change), S11 (no family change before acceptance, selectionStatus, actionStatus, recommendedFamily), S13 (appraisal payload), D5 (status text), and S10 with D27 (substantive audit content in studyRevision so the held reply is refused). The audit patch itself needs L1.6 (store defect at 875fe59). Catches: a model null erasing investigator constraints, a proposed family applied early, downstream stages left current after an upstream change, and a stale audit reply overwriting the investigator's notes.

inputs.need:
I am a health economist working with the cardiac surgery network of four hospitals in our province. Two of the four centres (A and B) started remote monitoring after cardiac surgery in March 2025: patients go home with a tablet, a blood pressure cuff, a scale and a single-lead ECG patch, and a nurse reviews the readings every day for 30 days. Centres C and D still use usual follow-up, a telephone call at one week and a clinic visit at six weeks. The ministry is deciding whether to fund remote monitoring at all four centres from 2028 and has asked us for a cost-effectiveness analysis.

The programme costs about 1,400 per patient for devices, the platform licence and nursing time. The hope is that it prevents readmissions and emergency visits in the first 30 to 90 days, which are common after surgery: about 14 percent of patients were readmitted within 30 days across the network last year. We have the provincial hospital discharge abstracts and physician billing for all four centres, the monitoring platform's own logs at A and B, and a costing unit that can price hospital episodes.

I need help deciding how to estimate the effect when centres chose whether to adopt it, which costs and outcomes to include, what time horizon makes sense, how to handle differences between centres in case mix and surgical volume, and how many patients we need. Our team is two economists and a data analyst, and the ministry wants the answer by June 2027.
inputs.constraints: Results needed by 2027-06-30 for the ministry. Two economists and one data analyst. Provincial data only through the data institute's secure environment; no patient contact.

Centre D's research office has not yet signed the addendum that would release its local cost ledger.

records.title: Remote monitoring after cardiac surgery and 30-day readmission: a randomised trial
records.authors: Lindberg-Asante K, Moreau-Obi T, Castellanos-Pryor J
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 610 adults discharged after cardiac surgery to 30 days of remote monitoring with daily nurse review of blood pressure, weight, rhythm and symptoms, or to usual follow-up. Thirty-day readmission was 9.2 percent with remote monitoring and 12.8 percent with usual care (risk ratio 0.72, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 1.10). Emergency department visits without admission were 11 percent and 17 percent. Atrial fibrillation was detected earlier with monitoring. Patients reported high satisfaction, and 8 percent stopped transmitting before day 30. The trial was not powered for readmission and did not collect costs.

records.title: Cost-effectiveness of remote monitoring after cardiac surgery: a model-based analysis
records.abstract: We built a decision model with a 90-day horizon and a health system perspective, taking the effect on readmission from a single randomised trial. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was 18,500 per quality-adjusted life year. In probabilistic analysis, remote monitoring had a 54 percent probability of being cost-effective at a threshold of 50,000 per quality-adjusted life year. Results were driven almost entirely by the readmission effect, whose confidence interval crossed no effect. The authors recommend a real-world comparison across hospitals to estimate the effect before funding decisions.

records.title: Variation in readmission after cardiac surgery across hospitals: the role of case mix and discharge practices
records.authors: Okonjo-Brandt P, Silva-Nakamura H, Reid-Adeyemi F
records.abstract: We studied 28,400 patients discharged after cardiac surgery from 12 hospitals over four years. Thirty-day readmission varied from 9 to 19 percent across hospitals. Case mix, including age, frailty, ejection fraction, urgency and procedure type, explained about half of the variation between hospitals. Hospitals with early follow-up calls had lower adjusted readmission, but the association was confounded by hospital volume. The authors warn that comparisons of programmes between hospitals must adjust for case mix and account for stable differences between hospitals.

records.title: Remote patient monitoring after surgery: a systematic review of readmission and emergency department visits
records.authors: Haugen-Mbeki A, Olsen-Carvalho R, Tan-Whitaker M
records.abstract: We included 21 studies of remote patient monitoring after surgery, 7 of them randomised. Across all studies, readmission was lower with monitoring (risk ratio 0.81, 95 percent CI 0.68 to 0.97), but the effect was smaller in randomised studies. In the cardiac surgery subgroup of 6 studies, the risk ratio was 0.84 (95 percent CI 0.64 to 1.10). Emergency department visits were reduced in most studies. Few studies reported costs, and none compared hospitals that adopted monitoring with hospitals that did not while accounting for trends before adoption.

records.title: Patients' and carers' experience of home monitoring after heart surgery: an interview study
records.abstract: We interviewed 20 patients and 12 carers after 30 days of home monitoring following cardiac surgery. Most described reassurance from knowing a nurse was reviewing their readings. Some found alerts about minor changes worrying and phoned the hospital more as a result. Older patients often depended on a carer to set up and use the devices. Several patients in rural areas lost connection for days. Participants wanted to know in advance what would happen when an alert fired, and carers asked for a named contact at the hospital.

records.title: Comparing adopting and non-adopting hospitals in health services evaluation: difference-in-differences with few sites
records.abstract: We examine methods for estimating programme effects when a few hospitals adopt a programme and others do not. Differences between hospitals that are stable over time can be removed by comparing changes before and after adoption, but only if outcomes followed parallel trends before adoption. With only two adopting and two comparison hospitals, conventional standard errors are far too small; a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference gives honest intervals. Contamination, when a comparison hospital adopts part of the programme, biases the estimate towards no effect and should be handled by ending the comparison period at the contamination date.

records.title: Health system costs in the 90 days after discharge from cardiac surgery
records.abstract: We priced all health system contacts in the 90 days after discharge for 9,800 cardiac surgery patients using provincial case costing. The mean cost after discharge was 6,200 per patient. Readmissions accounted for 58 percent of this cost, emergency department visits for 9 percent and physician visits for 14 percent. Costs were highest for patients readmitted with infection or heart failure. Costs of home care and medications were not included because they are not held in the provincial data, so total costs are understated.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One randomised trial and a systematic review suggest remote monitoring after cardiac surgery lowers readmission and emergency visits, but the cardiac estimates have intervals that include no effect. A model-based economic evaluation found cost-effectiveness to be close to a coin toss because it borrowed that imprecise effect. Readmission varies widely between hospitals, half of it explained by case mix, and methods work shows that comparisons of few adopting and non-adopting hospitals need before-and-after contrasts, honest few-cluster intervals and a rule for contamination. Readmissions drive most post-discharge cost. The missing input for the ministry is a fair real-world effect estimate with costs attached.
response.gradeRationale: Effect evidence imprecise and partly non-randomised; economic evidence rests on a single imprecise trial; methods guidance is strong but not an effect estimate.

response.reading: The ministry's question is economic, but the decisive unknown is the effect of monitoring on readmission in this network. Centres chose whether to adopt, differ in case mix and volume, and one comparison centre has started a small pilot. Provincial data cover all four centres before and after adoption, which allows a cohort comparison of changes with costs attached. Patient burden and carer dependence shape adherence and therefore effect.

response.rationale: The ministry asked for a cost-effectiveness analysis, but the analysis is only as good as its effect estimate: the trial's interval includes no effect (c1) and the existing model is close to a coin toss because it borrowed that estimate (c2). A four-centre cohort built from provincial data, comparing changes before and after March 2025 at adopting and comparison centres with adjustment for case mix (c3) and few-cluster inference with a contamination rule (c4), produces the effect estimate and attaches provincial costs (c5), so cost per readmission avoided can be computed within the same cohort. A model-based economic evaluation stays as a later step if the ministry wants a longer horizon.

response.designSummary: Cohort with a difference-in-differences contrast between two adopting and two comparison centres, 2023 to 2026, and a within-cohort cost analysis.
response.sampleSize: About 3,650 exposed discharges at A and B and about 2,900 comparison discharges at C and D are expected after March 2025. An individual-level comparison would detect a fall in 30-day readmission from 14 to 11 percent with 90 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 with about 2,550 patients per group, so patient numbers are sufficient. The binding limit is the number of centres: with four clusters, intervals from a wild cluster bootstrap will be wide, and the report will present the estimate with that interval rather than a significance verdict.
response.primaryAnalysis: Logistic difference-in-differences model of 30-day readmission with centre and quarter fixed effects, the seven case-mix covariates, and an adoption-by-period term; wild cluster bootstrap intervals; an event-study version to check pre-adoption trends.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Generalised linear model with gamma distribution for 90-day cost; cost per readmission avoided from the two contrasts with a joint bootstrap; emergency visits; subgroups by age over 80 and rurality.
response.missingData: Linked provincial records are complete for admissions; platform logs missing for some days are reported; centre D's local costs are replaced by provincial case costing if the ledger is not released.
response.multiplicity: One primary contrast; others are reported with intervals as secondary.

response.designSummary: Cohort with a difference-in-differences contrast between two adopting and two comparison centres, 2023 to 2026, and a within-cohort cost analysis.
response.sampleSize: After ending centre C's comparison period at June 2026, about 3,650 exposed and about 2,475 comparison discharges are expected. The harmonic mean group size is about 2,950, still above the about 2,550 per group needed to detect a fall from 14 to 11 percent with 90 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05. The number of centres is unchanged, so centre-level inference remains the binding limit and intervals come from a wild cluster bootstrap.
response.primaryAnalysis: Logistic difference-in-differences model of 30-day readmission with centre and quarter fixed effects, the seven case-mix covariates, and an adoption-by-period term; wild cluster bootstrap intervals; an event-study version to check pre-adoption trends.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Generalised linear model with gamma distribution for 90-day cost; cost per readmission avoided from the two contrasts with a joint bootstrap; emergency visits; subgroups by age over 80 and rurality.
response.missingData: As before; centre C's discharges from July 2026 are excluded from the comparison group, and the 40 pilot patients are described separately.
response.multiplicity: One primary contrast; others are reported with intervals as secondary.
response.software: R within the data institute's environment; code archived before linkage.
overfittingGuards: No data-driven choice of comparison centres

response.title: Remote monitoring after cardiac surgery across four centres: a cohort study of readmission and cost
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the effect of remote monitoring after cardiac surgery on 30-day readmission and 90-day cost, and the cost per readmission avoided. Design: four-centre cohort from provincial data, 2023 to 2026, with before-and-after contrasts between adopting and comparison centres. Results will follow analysis.
response.introduction: Remote monitoring after surgery may prevent readmissions, but estimates are imprecise and economic models borrow them.
response.methods: Provincial discharge abstracts, billing and platform logs; difference-in-differences with case-mix adjustment; wild cluster bootstrap; centre C's comparison period ends at its pilot.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet.
response.discussion: The discussion will set the estimate against the trial and review and explain what the four-centre design can and cannot show.
response.limitations: Four centres; non-random adoption; missing home care and medication costs.
response.reportingChecklist: STROBE with RECORD; CHEERS 2022 for the cost analysis
